The analysis focuses on the popular factorized velocity setting with mixture paths, parameterized by Transformer architectures. The paper provides end-to-end guarantees that the generated distribution provably converges to the true data distribution as training samples increase.

Detailed proofs provided in appendices, demonstrating technical thoroughness
Theoretical justification for factorized velocities as statistically beneficial beyond computational convenience is a valuable insight

The analysis covers both factorized velocities (the practically common setting) and general velocity fields, with the factorized setting showing improved dependence on vocabulary size. The paper bridges a critical gap between the empirical success of DFM and its theoretical understanding, providing formal justification for using Transformers in discrete flow matching.

Honest discussion of limitations, particularly the polynomial dependence on vocabulary size which the authors acknowledge makes the bounds impractical for large-vocabulary tasks
Rigorous proofs provided in extensive appendices

Lack of any experimental validation or numerical illustrations of the theoretical rates, making it difficult to assess whether the bounds are tight or overly pessimistic

Significant presentation issues: duplicated theorem statements in the main text, sections appearing multiple times, the paper title appears as '1 Introduction', and the paper is excessively long (81.4k tokens) with much restatement of prior work

The connection between the theoretical setup and practical DFM implementations is somewhat loose; for instance, the time interval clipping [t0,T] and the specific assumptions on the mixture path may not align with all practical implementations
Some technical details appear questionable, such as the treatment of the factorized velocity decomposition in the error bounds and the handling of the exponential term exp(M_u) in Theorem 3.1
The paper does not provide any discussion of how the theoretical insights could guide practical algorithm design or hyperparameter selection

Could you comment on whether this rate is an artifact of the proof technique (e.g., the covering number approach or the Grönwall argument) or is it believed to be fundamental? Are there any lower bounds that suggest this rate is tight?
